findings.headline: The five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures, with the paper stating this as its policy on bids for growth and service investment.
findings.detail: The paper states that the policy on bids for growth and service investment is that the five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures only. This sets the scope of what the MTFS will fund beyond existing commitments.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing councils' budget-setting policies will want to know whether discretionary growth bids are funded, since this determines how much headroom exists for new service pressures.
findings.quote: The five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures only.

findings.headline: Government Revenue Support Grant is assumed at nil and New Homes Bonus has been revoked from 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper's assumptions table records Government Grant for RSG as nil and states that New Homes Bonus was revoked in 2025/26. These two items are set out as the baseline for the 2027/28 strategy.
findings.matters: A council with no RSG and no New Homes Bonus depends more heavily on council tax, business rates and fees, which is a position other councils managing funding losses will compare against.
findings.figures: RSG £nil, New Homes Bonus revoked 2025/26
findings.quote: Government Grant - RSG Nil

findings.headline: Renewable energy income from NNDR is assumed to rise from £3,739,600 in 2026/27 to £4,334,000 in 2031/32.
findings.detail: The paper sets out a forecast schedule of NNDR renewable energy income, with figures of £3,739,600 for 2026/27, £3,969,000 for 2027/28, £4,045,000 for 2028/29, £4,146,000 for 2029/30, £4,249,000 for 2030/31 and £4,334,000 for 2031/32.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with renewable generation in its tax base will recognise the sensitivity of a single income stream to the assumed trajectory.

findings.headline: Our Environment Reserve contribution from the general fund is set at £1.1m for 2026/27, falling to £600k in 2027/28 and ceasing from 2031/32, funded by assumed grant income.
findings.detail: The paper states the contribution is currently £1.1m for 2026/27 and is to reduce to £600k in 2027/28, £450k in 2028/29, £300k in 2029/30 and £150k in 2030/31, ceasing from 2031/32. It notes that the reduction is funded by assumed grant income receivable.
findings.matters: The reserve's general fund contributions depend on grant income not yet confirmed, so the council's ability to sustain environment-related spending over the period rests on that assumption.

findings.headline: Employer pension contribution rates fall from 1 April 2026 following the October 2025 triennial review, with the secondary rate reduced to nil.
findings.detail: The paper says the triennial review was completed in October 2025 and that the primary rate decreased from 23.6% to 17.6% from 01/04/26. It states that the secondary rate was reduced by £416k to nil. The last triennial valuation applies for 2026/27 to 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lower employer contribution rate reduces a major establishment cost for the council, and other councils in the same pension fund cycle will be watching how the rate change feeds through their own budgets.
findings.quote: Primary Rate decreased from 23.6% to 17.6% effective 01/04/26. Secondary rate reduced £416k to £nil.

findings.headline: The General Fund Balance is shown at £1,800,000 at the opening and at every year-end through to 2031/32, with no movements.
findings.detail: The General Fund Balance row has no contributions or drawdowns in any year, so the balance is shown unchanged across the period.
findings.matters: A general fund balance held flat for the full period is a benchmark other councils and lenders would compare against their own unallocated reserves.
findings.figures: £1,800,000 at opening and at each year-end shown
findings.quote: General Fund Balance 1,800,000

findings.headline: The Covid Recovery reserve of £254,930 is drawn in full in year one, leaving nil.
findings.detail: The table shows the full opening balance taken out in year one, with no contributions and no closing balance from that year onward.
findings.matters: A pandemic-era reserve fully spent down is a clear marker of a funding source that no longer exists for other councils to rely on.
findings.figures: Opening £254,930; year one drawdown (£254,930); closing nil
findings.quote: Covid Recovery 254,930

findings.headline: The New Homes Bonus reserve opens at £3,710,695 and is drawn by £1,323,700 in year one and £2,300,000 in year two, leaving £86,995.
findings.detail: The reserve is used over the first two years and is then held at £86,995 for the remaining years in the table.
findings.matters: Other councils that have relied on New Homes Bonus income will want to see how quickly this reserve is being used up.
findings.figures: Opening £3,710,695; year one drawdown (£1,323,700); year two drawdown (£2,300,000); closing £86,995
findings.quote: New Homes Bonus 3,710,695

findings.headline: The Financial Resilience reserve opens at £1,546,167 and falls to £259,067 after drawdowns of £512,200 in year one and £1,074,900 in year two.
findings.detail: The reserve is drawn down in the first two years and then held at £259,067 for the remaining years shown. Year one also includes a £300,000 contribution.
findings.matters: A council whose financial resilience reserve is being run down is one a finance director or lender would want to track against its medium-term budget gap.
findings.figures: Opening £1,546,167; year one contribution £300,000; year one drawdown (£512,200); year two drawdown (£1,074,900); closing £259,067
findings.quote: Financial Resilience 1,546,167

findings.headline: The Income Volatility reserve opens at £9,757,711 and is drawn by £1,506,400 in year one and £4,387,600 in year two, after a £5,000,000 contribution in year two.
findings.detail: The reserve is built and drawn in both directions over the period. The first-year closing balance is £8,565,311 and the second-year closing balance is £9,177,711.
findings.matters: A reserve set aside to absorb income shortfalls is directly relevant to how other councils are protecting themselves against income volatility.
findings.figures: Opening £9,757,711; year one drawdown (£1,506,400); year two contribution £5,000,000; year two drawdown (£4,387,600); year two closing £9,177,711
findings.quote: Income Volatility 9,757,711

findings.headline: The LGR Transitional Costs reserve receives £2,500,000 in each of the first two years and reaches nil after £5,000,000 is drawn in the second year.
findings.detail: The reserve starts at nil. The paper shows £2,500,000 added in year one and £2,500,000 added in year two, with (£5,000,000) drawn in year two, leaving a closing balance of nil.
findings.matters: Other councils going through local government reorganisation will want to compare how transitional costs are being funded and when the reserve is spent down.
findings.figures: Year one contributions £2,500,000; year two contributions £2,500,000; year two drawdown (£5,000,000); closing balance nil
findings.quote: LGR Transitional Costs -

findings.headline: North Kesteven's total usable reserves open at £39,185,527, and the first year shows £29,276,930 drawn against £20,724,200 added, closing at £30,632,797.
findings.detail: The Total Usable Reserves row shows opening, contributions (To), drawdowns (From) and closing balances for each year. The first-year drawdown is larger than the contributions, so the closing balance is lower than the opening balance.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender comparing reserve cover across councils needs the size and pace of drawdown from the total usable reserves figure.
findings.figures: Opening £39,185,527; first-year contributions £20,724,200; first-year drawdown (£29,276,930); first-year closing £30,632,797
findings.quote: Total Usable Reserves 39,185,527

findings.headline: Our Environment reserve contributions fall from £1,052,100 in 2026/27 to nil in 2031/32, in £150,000 steps after 2027/28
findings.detail: The Our Environment row starts at £1,052,100, then £600,000, £450,000, £300,000, £150,000 and nil. The Climate row separately shows £300,000 in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28, then nil.
findings.matters: A finance officer tracking how a council funds environmental and climate commitments can compare a fixed multi-year schedule of reserve top-ups with their own.
findings.quote: Our Environment 1,052,100.00

findings.headline: Total reserve contributions fall from £5,252,100 in 2026/27 to £1,525,000 in 2031/32
findings.detail: The totals row gives £5,252,100 for 2026/27, £4,925,000 for 2027/28, £1,975,000 for 2028/29, £1,825,000 for 2029/30, £1,675,000 for 2030/31 and £1,525,000 for 2031/32. The 2026/27 total is the first column, marked 'Approved', and the rest are marked 'Forecast'.
findings.matters: The fall in annual contributions shows how much of the planned reserve funding is concentrated in the first two years, which affects how much cover the council expects to build from its own resources later on.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation reserve is set to receive £2,500,000 in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28, with no contribution from 2028/29
findings.detail: The Local Government Reorganisation row shows £2,500,000 in each of the first two years and a dash in each year from 2028/29 to 2031/32. The 2026/27 column is headed 'Approved' and the later columns 'Forecast'.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council facing reorganisation costs can compare how much this council has set aside and over what period.
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation 2,500,000.00

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: HRA new-build schemes of £50.1 million remain to be planned, against a 40-year payback criterion that the paper says rising development costs make increasingly challenging
findings.detail: The paper says the ten-year HRA capital programme includes £50.1 million for new-build schemes that remain to be planned. The Council's value-for-money criterion is that a new-build scheme should pay back within 40 years. The paper says each scheme will need robust appraisal before approval.
findings.matters: Rising development costs reducing scheme viability against a fixed payback test is a constraint that other housing-led councils and their lenders would weigh.
findings.figures: £50.1 million for new-build schemes; 40-year payback criterion
findings.quote: Rising development costs have made this increasingly challenging

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Internal audit returned to an in-house service in October 2025, after Lincolnshire Assurance ceased providing it in September 2025
findings.detail: The paper states that the internal audit service became an in-house service in October 2025. It says Lincolnshire Assurance stopped providing the service in September 2025. The Council's internal audit is required to meet the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015.
findings.matters: A change in internal audit provider close to a financial year-end is a control change that a finance director at another council would want to know about when reviewing their own arrangements.
findings.quote: internal audit service returned to being an in-house service in October 2025

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The external auditor's Auditor's Annual Report for the year ended 31 March 2025 states the Council has adequate arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness
findings.detail: The paper quotes the external auditor's latest Auditor's Annual Report for the year ended 31 March 2025. It records that the auditor found adequate arrangements in place to improve the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of services. The paper also says the internal audit service returned to being in-house in October 2025.
findings.matters: A value-for-money conclusion from the external auditor is a governance signal that lenders and peers look for in a council's annual audit outcome.
findings.quote: the Council have adequate arrangements in place to improve the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of services

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The Council has set aside a reserve to dampen the impact of Local Government Reorganisation if it is implemented later
findings.detail: The paper says the Government paused the Local Government Reorganisation programme in September 2026. It says the Council has set aside a reserve that will help dampen the expected negative impact if reorganisation proceeds at a later date. The paper does not give the reserve's value in Annex A.
findings.matters: A council that sets aside a reserve specifically for a reorganisation transition is making a provision that other councils facing the same reform would want to compare.
findings.quote: has set aside a reserve, which will help dampen the expected negative impact if reorganisation is implemented at a later date

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The 2026/27 pay award is settled at 3.3%, which the paper says was higher than expected
findings.detail: The paper states that the pay award for 2026/27 has been settled at 3.3% and was a higher increase than expected. It describes the Council's workforce as its largest expense. The paper identifies future pay increases as a particular risk.
findings.matters: A pay award above budget assumptions adds to the cost base of the largest expense line, and other councils would compare their own settlements against this figure.
findings.quote: the pay award has been settled for 2026/27 at 3.3%

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The paper identifies refinancing rates as a material uncertainty over the strategy period, with Lafford Homes loan assumptions to be refreshed in the 2027/28 NK Financial Plan
findings.detail: The paper says actual Lafford Homes loan drawdowns may vary from the capital programme profile, which affects interest on both investments and borrowing. It states that external borrowing need is based on projected cashflows. The borrowing and interest assumptions will be refreshed after the Lafford Homes Business Plan is revised in November 2026.
findings.matters: Refinancing rates feeding into both council borrowing and Lafford Homes loan income are a direct exposure for a lender and a council finance director to track.
findings.quote: Refinancing rates remain a material uncertainty over the strategy period

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: £93.0 million of the £111.7 million ten-year Lafford Homes funding relates to schemes that are not yet fully planned
findings.detail: The paper says £18.7 million of the Lafford Homes funding relates to schemes being delivered, and £93.0 million relates to schemes that are not yet fully planned. The company's 2027/28 Business Plan will refine the development programme. The paper also says Lafford Homes' capital is supported by an agreed schedule of loan principal repayments.
findings.matters: The split between delivered and unplanned schemes indicates how much of a council's lending and capital exposure to its own housing company is still undecided, which affects both the council's risk and any lender's view of that exposure.
findings.figures: £111.7 million total; £18.7 million for delivered schemes; £93.0 million not yet fully planned
findings.quote: £93.0 million relates to schemes that are not yet fully planned

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The ten-year capital programme of £299.6 million is described as fully funded at programme level
findings.detail: The paper states that the indicative programme for 2027/28 to 2036/37 totals £299.6 million. It is split into £162.3 million of General Fund and £137.3 million of HRA investment. The paper says the programme combines schemes already being delivered with proposals still subject to planning and business cases.
findings.matters: Describing a programme as fully funded while a large part of it is still in planning shows what a council considers committed, and lenders and peers would look at how much of the total is firm.
findings.figures: £299.6 million total; £162.3 million General Fund; £137.3 million HRA
findings.quote: fully funded at programme level, comprising £162.3 million of General Fund investment and £137.3 million of Housing Revenue Account investment

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: HRA forecast deficit for 2026/27 is £0.043m as at 30 June 2026, with the HRA still expected to contribute to its working balance
findings.detail: The paper says the Housing Revenue Account is forecast to make a contribution to its working balance despite the deficit. This is expected to keep the working balance at around its £1.0m target by 31 March 2027. The deficit follows delays in full contract mobilisation, which led to reliance on alternative contractors.
findings.matters: A small HRA deficit that is absorbed within the working balance, and the cause given for it, shows how a housing contractor mobilisation delay flows into the HRA.
findings.figures: deficit of £0.043m for 2026/27; HRA Working Balance target of around £1.0m
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026, a deficit of £0.043m is forecast for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Renewable energy business rates of an estimated £3.7million per annum are retained by NKDC and treated as outside the scope of the planned reforms
findings.detail: The paper says the renewable energy business rates are 100% retained where the Council approves the planning permission. It says this income is currently outside the scope of the planned local government finance reforms. If the scope changed, there could be a partial or full loss of the income to the General Fund, but the MTFS assumes it continues.
findings.matters: Renewable energy business rates are a significant income line for a district council, and a change in scope would hit the General Fund directly, which other councils with similar renewable schemes would want to track.
findings.figures: £3.7million per annum
findings.quote: amount to an estimated £3.7million per annum

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Savings achieved under the Financial Sustainability programme total £3.5m per annum as at March 2025
findings.detail: The paper refers back to the 27 March 2025 Executive Board report. It states that savings achieved to date under the Financial Sustainability programme were £3.5m per annum as at March 2025. The Council is now running a further programme to identify recurring savings and income.
findings.matters: A council's delivered savings to date, set against the target it has set itself, shows whether its savings programme is landing, and a peer can use the figure as a benchmark.
findings.figures: £3.5m per annum
findings.quote: the savings already achieved to date, as at March 2025, amount to £3.5m per annum

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: The MTFS forecasts a balanced five-year General Fund budget to 2031/32, with balance maintained through Income Volatility Reserve appropriations and drawdowns
findings.detail: The paper says the strategy balances the five-year General Fund budget and that this is sustainable over the medium term through transfers to and from the Income Volatility Reserve. It also says the five-year General Fund position is much more challenging than the one-year position.
findings.matters: A balanced five-year forecast that depends on reserve movements is a different position from one balanced by recurring savings or income, and peers facing the same pressures would compare the two.
findings.quote: The MTFS forecasts a balanced five-year budget to 2031/32.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: General Fund deficits are funded from the Income Volatility Reserve, which the paper says "cannot continue indefinitely"
findings.detail: The paper states that the current funding of General Fund budget deficits comes from a drawdown from the Income Volatility Reserve. It describes this as one-off money that cannot continue indefinitely. The reserve is also the Council's primary mechanism for managing funding and expenditure volatility.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to know how much of a balanced budget depends on one-off reserve drawdowns rather than recurring income.
findings.quote: The current funding of budget deficits is sourced from a drawdown from the Income Volatility Reserve, which cannot continue indefinitely due to the one-off nature of these monies.

findings.headline: Average re-let time for council housing major works voids is off target in Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper lists KP052, average re-let time for council housing in calendar days for major works voids, as off target. No day count or target is given in the report; the detail sits on the online dashboard.
findings.matters: Longer void periods mean homes are empty for longer and not generating rent, which bears on the housing income a finance officer is budgeting for.
findings.figures: 11% (3) of indicators off target
findings.quote: KP052 Average re-let time for Council Housing (calendar days) - major works voids

findings.headline: Rent collection indicator KP079 is within variance in Quarter 2 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper lists two indicators as within variance in Quarter 2: KP079 on rent collected and KP080 on invoices paid within 30 days. The paper gives no rent collection percentage, so the figure it reports is the indicator's rating.
findings.matters: Rent collection is a direct income line for a council housing service, so a finance director, or a lender assessing that income, would want to see when it moves off target.
findings.figures: 7% (2) of indicators within variance
findings.quote: KP079 Rent collected as percentage of rent due

findings.headline: Transfer to Major Repairs Reserve forecast at £6,273,900 in 2027/28, peaking at £7,366,100 in 2030/31 and £7,043,200 in 2031/32
findings.detail: Repairs and maintenance spend is forecast at £6,513,300 in 2027/28, peaking at £7,060,400 in 2029/30 and falling to £6,890,600 in 2030/31, while the transfer to the Major Repairs Reserve rises that year. The paper does not explain the difference between the two movements.
findings.matters: The split between revenue repairs spend and transfers to the Major Repairs Reserve shows how much HRA income is directed to capital investment in the housing stock, which peers compare when planning stock investment.
findings.quote: Transfer to / (from) Major Repairs Reserve 6,273,900

findings.headline: Rental income forecast to rise from £21,063,000 in 2027/28 to £23,219,500 in 2031/32
findings.detail: Rental income is the largest line in the HRA, making up most of the total income of £21,172,400 in 2027/28. The paper does not set out the rent assumptions behind the increase.
findings.matters: Rent is the main HRA revenue source, so the planned rise underpins the forecast surplus and working balance, and peer councils will compare their own rent assumptions against it.
findings.quote: Rental Income (21,063,000)

findings.headline: Interest repayments forecast at £2,047,000 in 2027/28, falling to £1,954,700 in 2031/32
findings.detail: The line is £2,021,700 in 2028/29, £2,002,600 in 2029/30, £2,017,900 in 2030/31 and £1,954,700 in 2031/32. The paper does not explain the movements or name any borrowing decision behind them.
findings.matters: Interest is a fixed charge on HRA revenue, so a finance director at another council would compare this trajectory with their own debt profile.
findings.quote: Interest Repayments 2,047,000

findings.headline: HRA closing working balance forecast at £1,100,000 from 2027/28 to 2030/31, rising to £1,200,000 in 2031/32
findings.detail: The paper shows a net operating surplus of £126,200 in 2027/28 and £100,000 in 2031/32, with nil in 2028/29 to 2030/31. The opening working balance for 2027/28 is £973,800, so the first year lifts it to £1,100,000.
findings.matters: Peers and lenders compare planned HRA working balances across councils to judge how much headroom each HRA has against cost or income shocks.
findings.figures: Opening working balance 2027/28 £973,800; closing working balance £1,100,000 (2027/28 to 2030/31) and £1,200,000 (2031/32); net operating surplus £126,200 (2027/28) and £100,000 (2031/32)
findings.quote: Closing Working Balance (1,100,000)

findings.headline: Other capital charges are £6,895,900 in 2027/28, against £1,931,000 in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The Other Capital Charges line is the largest single capital charge in 2027/28 and falls sharply the following year. This appendix does not give the reason for the change in that line.
findings.matters: A one-year spike in capital charges of this size is the kind of line a finance director would expect a note on, and a peer council would want to know the cause of.

findings.headline: Interest payments rise from £3,740,300 in 2027/28 to £4,793,400 in 2031/32, while investment interest rises from £(4,956,100) to £(6,327,700).
findings.detail: Within the capital charges and investments section, interest payments increase in every year of the forecast. Investment interest income also increases over the period, with the paper showing both lines in brackets for income.
findings.matters: A rising gross interest cost on the General Fund is a borrowing position a lender and a finance director would both want to track against the funding assumed in the same forecast.

findings.headline: Support grants in the financing section fall from £4,519,400 in 2027/28 to £3,577,000 in 2029/30, while council tax rises from £8,512,600 to £10,047,400 over the same five years.
findings.detail: The Financed By section shows support grants declining to 2029/30 and then rising slightly to £3,739,000 in 2031/32. Council tax rises in every year, and business rates rise from £7,141,000 to £7,745,000.
findings.matters: The shift in the funding mix from government grant towards council tax is the funding change a finance director at another council would compare against their own grant reductions.

findings.headline: North Kesteven's General Fund (Surplus) / Deficit is shown as nil in each year from 2027/28 to 2031/32, with reserve appropriations of (5,206,200) in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The summary records the General Fund (Surplus) / Deficit as nil in all five years. Reserve appropriations vary across the period, from (5,206,200) in 2027/28 to (482,700) in 2028/29, and net expenditure is financed by council tax, business rates and support grants.
findings.matters: A nil position in every year that depends on reserve appropriations of this size is one a finance director, here or at another council, would test against the reserve balances behind it.
findings.figures: Reserve Appropriations: £(5,206,200) 2027/28; £(482,700) 2028/29; £(2,244,400) 2029/30; £(1,526,300) 2030/31; £(1,998,700) 2031/32 (bracketed in the paper). General Fund (Surplus) / Deficit: nil in each year.

findings.headline: HRA decarbonisation works total £14,630,300 over 2027/28 to 2030/31, with £6,508,200 in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Decarbonisation works are listed as a delivered Housing Revenue Account scheme. The annual amounts fall from £6,508,200 in 2027/28 to £1,611,100 in 2030/31 and are zero thereafter.
findings.matters: A large delivered energy-efficiency programme with a fixed end date affects the HRA's spending profile and the cost of meeting net-zero obligations, which other housing landlords are also facing.
findings.quote: Decarbonisation works

findings.headline: Sleaford Moor Enterprise Park future phases are planned at £22,745,600 over 2027/28 to 2031/32.
findings.detail: The paper lists future phases of Sleaford Moor Enterprise Park as a General Fund planned scheme, with annual amounts of £5,785,200 in 2027/28 and £4,300,000 in 2028/29, falling to zero after 2031/32.
findings.matters: Commercial development spend funded by the General Fund is a category where returns depend on occupancy and sales, so its ten-year profile is of interest to lenders and peers running similar enterprise schemes.
findings.quote: Sleaford Moor Enterprise Park (SMEP) - Future phases

findings.headline: Schemes at planning stage total £51,030,000 in the Housing Revenue Account and £121,795,600 in the General Fund over ten years.
findings.detail: The paper separates schemes being delivered from schemes being planned. The General Fund planned total is £121,795,600, with the largest amounts in 2027/28 to 2029/30. The HRA planning-stage total is £51,030,000, most of which is the New Homes General Build Programme unallocated budget.
findings.matters: Planning-stage schemes carry more uncertainty over cost and timing than schemes already being delivered, so the proportion of the programme in that stage is relevant to anyone assessing deliverability.
findings.figures: £51,030,000 (HRA planning stage, ten-year); £121,795,600 (General Fund planning stage, ten-year); £13,950,000 (HRA planning, 2027/28)
findings.quote: Total General Fund schemes being planned

findings.headline: Total capital programme is £299,583,200 over ten years, falling from £51,738,500 in 2027/28 to £15,291,700 in 2036/37.
findings.detail: The paper shows the programme peaking in 2027/28 and 2028/29 at £51,738,500 and £50,671,100. Totals fall to £28,338,000 in 2030/31 and to £15,291,700 by 2036/37, with HRA and General Fund totals of £137,286,000 and £162,297,200 respectively.
findings.matters: The shape of the profile shows when the largest funding requirements fall, which a finance director needs to match against borrowing and reserves over the same period.
findings.quote: Total Capital Programme

findings.headline: Lafford Homes unallocated schemes funding is planned at £81,300,000 over 2027/28 to 2033/34, the largest planned General Fund line in the programme.
findings.detail: The paper lists Lafford Homes unallocated schemes funding as a planned General Fund item, with annual amounts from £12,300,000 in 2027/28 to £7,000,000 in 2033/34. Separately, Lafford Homes development schemes funding appears in both the delivered (£18,653,800) and planned (£11,750,000) sections.
findings.matters: A large ten-year sum held as unallocated funding means the council's commitment to the programme depends on schemes not yet specified, which matters to lenders and to peers assessing similar housing company or development vehicles.
findings.quote: Lafford Homes - Unallocated schemes funding

findings.headline: Planned 2026/27 unit costs for the main local council expenditure headings are lower than the council's designated nearest neighbours and the England average, according to the LG Futures benchmarking.
findings.detail: The unit cost comparison is based on planned 2026/27 expenditure and covers designated nearest neighbours and the England average. The paper says the council will use these results to inform service reviews. The benchmarking table itself is not reproduced in the text supplied, so no individual unit cost figures are given here.
findings.matters: Peer finance officers using the same LG Futures toolkit can compare these benchmarking results with their own unit costs, and a lender would see how the council expects its service reviews to proceed.
findings.quote: the Council’s unit costs for the main local council expenditure headings are both lower than the designated nearest neighbours but also the average England position.

findings.headline: The paper rates financial governance as operating effectively but says the risk 'remains manageable but warrants continued oversight', citing financial complexity, organisational change and governance capacity.
findings.detail: The paper says governance is supported by the Audit Committee, Section 151 Officer, Internal Audit and External Audit. It also says increasing financial complexity, organisational change and the need to maintain governance and financial management capacity mean ongoing monitoring and improvement are required.
findings.matters: Governance capacity and organisational change are pressures a finance director at another council would recognise, and a lender would want to see whether the council's own assessment of that risk is being acted on.
findings.quote: The risk remains manageable but warrants continued oversight.

findings.headline: The paper says the council is 'maintaining and building key reserves', naming the Income Volatility Reserve, as part of moving away from the stress warning signs CIPFA identifies.
findings.detail: The paper presents reserve building, savings delivery and a reduced projected funding gap as the council's response to CIPFA's financial stress indicators. It names the Income Volatility Reserve as an example of a reserve being maintained and built.
findings.matters: A council that is rebuilding a volatility reserve while reserves are low against peers is a specific policy choice that other finance officers and lenders can compare with their own approach to income risk.
findings.quote: from maintaining and building key reserves (eg Income Volatility Reserve)

findings.headline: The paper describes North Kesteven's reserve levels as 'considered low' compared with other local councils, while General Fund and HRA balances are held at the council's stated minimum levels.
findings.detail: The paper states that reserves are planned, with General Fund and HRA balances in line with minimum levels the council has set, and that earmarked reserves are held only for specific purposes. It also says the council's policy is to keep reserves and balances low but prudent, so money is not left dormant.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to know how a council with low reserves against its peers is managing its risk, and a lender would weigh the same point when assessing headroom against financial shocks.
findings.quote: The Council’s reserve levels are considered low when compared to other local councils.

findings.headline: The Ombudsman's compensation orders are shown in the paper as £850, £250 and £200 across the categories of responsive repairs, managing relations and ASB.
findings.detail: The compensation chart lists three amounts for the period, shown against the categories of responsive repairs, managing relations and ASB/abuse/nuisance. The chart does not clearly map each amount to its category, and the paper's headline compensation figure is printed as '£1,3000'.
findings.matters: Compensation is a direct cash cost to the council, and the amounts show the scale of direct payments arising from housing complaints in the period.

findings.headline: The Ombudsman recorded 6 maladministration findings out of 8 for North Kesteven District Council, a maladministration rate of 75.0%.
findings.detail: The paper reports 3 determinations and 9 findings for the year, with 1 finding excluded as outside jurisdiction. The maladministration rate is calculated from the 6 maladministration findings against 8 countable findings.
findings.matters: Maladministration findings carry redress costs and reputational exposure, and a finance director at another council can compare the rate against their own housing complaints record.
findings.figures: 6 maladministration findings; 8 findings; 75.0% maladministration rate; 3 determinations; 9 findings
findings.quote: The number of 'Mal' findings recorded for North Kesteven District Council is 6, which gives the Maladministration rate of 75.0% (6 / 8).

findings.headline: All 12 Housing Ombudsman orders on 2025-26 determinations were recorded as complied with within three months, 100%.
findings.detail: The paper's order compliance table records 12 orders with target dates in the period, all marked as complied. The orders arise from three determinations with 9 findings in total.
findings.matters: A finance director can see that the redress and remedial obligations arising from these complaints were met on time, with no outstanding order liabilities reported.
findings.figures: 12 orders; 100% complied
findings.quote: Complied 12 100%

findings.headline: Financial projections beyond 2027/28 are described by the paper as indicative and subject to material revision
findings.detail: The paper says the projections beyond 2027/28 should be regarded as indicative and subject to material revision once the outcome of the Government's review and any revised implementation timetable are known. It also says the funding figures for 2028/29 and beyond are indicative and subject to review in the 2028 spending review.
findings.matters: A medium-term plan whose later years are explicitly provisional limits how far the reserve and funding assumptions can be relied on by a reader beyond the next budget.
findings.figures: Projections indicative beyond 2027/28; funding for 2028/29 onward indicative
findings.quote: projections beyond 2027/28 should be regarded as indicative

findings.headline: The Secretary of State announced a rapid review of the national LGR programme on 7 September 2026, and implementation activity has been paused
findings.detail: The paper says the future structure, geography and timetable for Greater Lincolnshire remain uncertain. The MTFS therefore assumes North Kesteven continues as it is, and projections beyond 2027/28 are described as indicative.
findings.matters: A council planning on the assumption that it continues unchanged, with indicative projections beyond 2027/28, is carrying a restructuring risk that lenders and peer finance teams will want to track.
findings.figures: Review announced 7 September 2026
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026, the Secretary of State announced a rapid review of the national LGR programme

findings.headline: The Lincolnshire Business Rates Pool was revoked by MHCLG for 2026/27 and all future years, after South Kesteven withdrew
findings.detail: South Kesteven District Council told North Kesteven it would withdraw from the pool for 2026/27. MHCLG then revoked the pool for 2026/27 and all future financial years, as the paper records.
findings.matters: Loss of a business rates pool removes a pooling gain that other councils in pools may face, and it changes the rates income assumptions for the medium term.
findings.figures: Notification received 2 February 2026; revocation applies to 2026/27 and all future financial years
findings.quote: Following this communication, the Council received notification from MHCLG on 2 February 2026

findings.headline: The Council is undertaking a review of its cost base and income-generating opportunities to reduce reliance on diminishing government funding
findings.detail: The paper describes a comprehensive review as the response to the funding reduction. It does not quantify any savings or income targets from the review in this report.
findings.matters: A cost and income review is the main mitigation for a funding loss, and the absence of a quantified target means the council's savings position cannot yet be assessed.
findings.quote: the Council is undertaking a comprehensive review of its cost base

findings.headline: The Income Volatility Reserve is forecast to hold £0.746million at 31 March 2032
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast is that the reserve will still hold a balance at the end of the planning period, after being deployed during the funding transition. The paper does not give the reserve's opening balance or the annual drawdowns.
findings.matters: The remaining balance at the end of the period shows how much headroom the council expects to have once the funding transition is complete.
findings.figures: £0.746million at 31 March 2032
findings.quote: The forecast is that the Income Volatility Reserve will retain a balance of £0.746million at 31 March 2032.

findings.headline: The MTFS sets a balanced 2027/28 position, with the Income Volatility Reserve used to support the medium term
findings.detail: The paper states the MTFS sets a balanced position for the coming year and a sustainable position over the medium term through use of the Income Volatility Reserve. It says the reserve will be deployed as necessary during the funding transition so services are not adversely affected.
findings.matters: Balancing the budget through a reserve drawdown rather than recurring savings or income is a specific route that finance directors and lenders will want to see tested against the funding loss.
findings.figures: Income Volatility Reserve forecast balance of £0.746million at 31 March 2032
findings.quote: The MTFS sets a balanced position for the coming year

findings.headline: North Kesteven forecasts an ongoing government funding reduction of approximately £780,000 per annum from 2027/28, after a one-off £557,900 grant in 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to the Fair Funding Review 2.0 and says the one-off Adjustment Support Grant cushioned only the immediate effect. The MTFS assumes the reduction continues into 2029/30 and beyond.
findings.matters: A recurring loss of around £780,000 a year in government funding is a structural gap that other councils absorbing Fair Funding 2.0 cuts will also be sizing against their own reserves and savings plans.
findings.figures: £780,000 per annum from 2027/28; cumulative loss of around £1.56 million by 2028/29; one-off Adjustment Support Grant of £557,900 in 2026/27
findings.quote: the Council is expected to experience an ongoing funding reduction of approximately £780,000 per annum from 2027/28, resulting in a cumulative loss of around £1.56 million by 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Final report - Localised Council Tax Support Scheme 2027-28
findings.headline: North Kesteven proposes a 'no change' Council Tax Support scheme for 2027/28, with more efficient UC-aligned options deferred until the local government reorganisation timeline is clearer
findings.detail: The paper considered a scheme aligned more closely to Universal Credit but rejected it for 2027/28. Reasons given include the need for significant modelling and testing of the NEC ICT system and the MHCLG guidance that current decisions should not fetter a future unitary council. The paper notes that the reorganisation timeline is uncertain after a review announced on 7 September 2026.
findings.matters: The decision to keep the scheme unchanged is shaped by local government reorganisation and by the cost of system change, which other councils facing unitary transitions will also weigh.
findings.quote: it is not considered appropriate to make any significant changes to the CTS scheme for 2027/28

findings.paper_title: Final report - Localised Council Tax Support Scheme 2027-28
findings.headline: North Kesteven has awarded £3,082 of Exceptional Hardship Payments in 2026/27 to the end of September 2026 and proposes a £25,000 budget for 2027/28
findings.detail: The Exceptional Hardship Payment scheme sits within Section 13A(1) of the Local Government Finance Act 1992. The paper says the council alone bears its cost. The proposed 2027/28 budget is set against the spend to date for 2026/27.
findings.matters: The cost falls wholly on the district rather than on the major precepting authorities, so a finance director at a peer council can compare the size of its own hardship budget against this one.
findings.figures: £3,082 awarded (2026/27 to end of September 2026); £25,000 proposed budget (2027/28)
findings.quote: As at the end of September 2026, a total of £3,082 EHP has been awarded for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Final report - Localised Council Tax Support Scheme 2027-28
findings.headline: North Kesteven's 2027/28 council tax modelling assumes a 98.5% collection rate, which the paper says is being reviewed
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy assumes a 98.5% collection rate for 2027/28. The paper says this assumption is being reviewed in light of current and previous collection levels. Modelling also assumes council tax increases of 1.9% and 2.9%, and caseload changes of zero and 2%.
findings.matters: A collection rate assumption that is under review directly affects the expected council tax yield, so finance officers at this council and at peers will watch whether the assumption is revised down.
findings.figures: 98.5% collection rate; council tax increases of 1.9% and 2.9%; caseload increase of 2%
findings.quote: this assumption is being reviewed as part of the development of the MTFS

findings.paper_title: Final report - Localised Council Tax Support Scheme 2027-28
findings.headline: North Kesteven's Council Tax Support caseload fell from 5,655 claimants in September 2021 to 5,344 in September 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the caseload peaked during the Covid-19 period and has since reduced and plateaued. Working-age claimants were 2,742 and pension-age claimants 2,602 at 30 September 2026. The paper states that the cost of the scheme is directly impacted by caseload and entitlement.
findings.matters: Caseload drives the cost of the discount scheme, which feeds the tax base and Collection Fund, so a finance director at this council or a peer can read it as a direct input to council tax income.
findings.figures: 5,655 claimants (September 2021); 5,344 claimants (September 2026); 2,742 working-age claimants; 2,602 pension-age claimants
findings.quote: the caseload has since reduced and plateaued (with some fluctuations)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: DRAFT Complaints Performance and Service Report
findings.headline: Damp and mould complaints (21 cases, 76.2% upheld) triggered Ombudsman-ordered capital remedial works (HHSRS inspection and repairs), creating committed expenditure obligation.
findings.detail: Damp and mould complaints totalled 21 cases (9% of 217 complaints), with 76.2% upheld (16 of 21). One Ombudsman determination (May 2025) specifically concerned damp, mould and complaint handling. The Ombudsman 'ordered the Council to undertake a full HHSRS inspection, complete any identified works' alongside £950 compensation. The high uphold rate combined with regulatory (HHSRS) remedial requirements creates non-discretionary capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Upheld housing health & safety complaints generate committed capital remedial works; Ombudsman-ordered works are mandatory expenditure obligations.
findings.figures: 21 damp and mould complaints (9% of 217); 76.2% upheld (16 of 21)
findings.quote: The Ombudsman ordered the Council to undertake a full HHSRS inspection, complete any identified works and make a compensation payment of £950, all of which were completed within the required timescales.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: DRAFT Complaints Performance and Service Report
findings.headline: Stage 1 investigation quality shows material weakness: 68.4% of complaints initially not upheld were subsequently upheld at Stage 2 review (13 of 19 cases).
findings.detail: The paper reports that 13 of 19 complaints not upheld at Stage 1 were overturned to upheld at Stage 2 review. This is presented as evidence of weakness: 'it also highlights the importance of continuing to strengthen Stage 1 investigations to ensure all relevant issues, evidence and customer impacts are fully explored at the earliest opportunity.' The high reversal rate indicates systemic issues in initial investigation quality or completeness.
findings.matters: High Stage 2 reversal rates drive escalation costs and create material risk of further Ombudsman referrals and compensation liability.
findings.figures: 13 of 19 initially not-upheld complaints reversed to upheld at Stage 2 (68.4%)
findings.quote: Importantly, 13 of the 19 complaints that were not upheld at Stage 1 were subsequently upheld at Stage 2 (68.4%). This demonstrates the value of the Stage 2 review process as an effective safeguard within complaint handling arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: DRAFT Complaints Performance and Service Report
findings.headline: 14.3% of Stage 1 complaints (31 cases) breached permitted response timescales, with 60.4% reliance on extension periods indicating resource or process constraints.
findings.detail: Of 217 Stage 1 complaints, only 25.3% were resolved within the 10-working-day standard; 60.4% required extensions to 20 days; 14.3% fell outside permitted timescales entirely. The paper acknowledges 'reliance on extensions remains significant and continues to be an area for improvement during 2026/27.' Ombudsman determinations identified timescale breaches as maladministration, citing 'delays in responding to service requests' and 'insufficient communication regarding those delays'.
findings.matters: Timescale breaches create Ombudsman escalation risk and indicate potential resource constraints or process inefficiency, with precedent from two 2025/26 upheld determinations.
findings.figures: 14.3% outside permitted timescales (31 complaints); 25.3% within 10-day standard
findings.quote: Overall, 25.3% of landlord complaints were resolved within the standard 10 working day timescale, with a further 60.4% responded to within an agreed extension period, resulting in 85.7% of complaints being responded to within permitted Complaint Handling Code timescales. The remaining 14.3% were responded to outside permitted timescales.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: DRAFT Complaints Performance and Service Report
findings.headline: Two of three Housing Ombudsman determinations upheld in 2025/26 finding maladministration, ordering £1,300 compensation and remedial works
findings.detail: Of three Ombudsman investigations completed in 2025/26, two were upheld. The first (May 2025) found 'maladministration in the Council's handling of concerns relating to windows and doors, damp and mould, and complaint handling' and ordered 'a full HHSRS inspection, complete any identified works' alongside £950 compensation. The second upheld determination (July 2025) on anti-social behaviour management found 'maladministration in both the handling of ASB reports and complaint handling' and ordered £350 compensation.
findings.matters: Upheld determinations create compensation liability precedent and reveal systemic process failures (delays, record-keeping, communication) indicating governance weaknesses beyond individual complaints.
findings.figures: 2 upheld determinations of 3 investigated; £1,300 total compensation (£950 + £350); Ombudsman-ordered HHSRS inspection and remedial works completion
findings.quote: The Ombudsman found maladministration in the Council's handling of concerns relating to windows and doors, damp and mould, and complaint handling, together with service failure relating to management of concerns about the heating system.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1: DRAFT Complaints Performance and Service Report
findings.headline: Ian Williams Ltd contractor accounted for 87 complaints (40% of all landlord complaints) in 2025/26, a notable increase from prior year, with Q4 volume indicating ongoing service delivery risk.
findings.detail: The paper reports that 87 complaints cited Ian Williams Ltd, representing 60% of all repairs complaints and 40% of all landlord complaints, described as 'a notable increase from 2024/25'. While the uphold rate has declined from 92% in Q1, volume remained elevated in Q4. The council notes: 'the volume of complaints received during Quarter 4 demonstrates that repairs service delivery and customer experience remain an area of risk and will continue to be subject to close oversight.'
findings.matters: Concentration of 40% of complaints with a single contractor represents material contract performance risk with implications for service continuity, tenant satisfaction, and contract management.
findings.figures: 87 complaints (60% of repairs complaints, 40% of all landlord complaints); Q1 uphold rate 92%
findings.quote: Of these repairs complaints, 87 specifically cited Ian Williams Ltd, representing 60% of all repairs complaints and 40% of all landlord complaints received during the year. This is a notable increase from 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rate improving, ahead of prior year by 1.67 percentage points, tracking in line with county and national trends
findings.detail: Cumulative Council Tax collection at 30 June 2026 is 30.38%, compared to 28.71% in the same period of the prior year—an improvement of 1.67 percentage points. The council notes this is 'in line with the wider county and national trends' and expects the full-year rate to remain close to prior-year levels. Council Tax is one of the council's two main funding sources.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the council's largest and most predictable income source; improvement in collection rate signals either improved resident compliance or effective collection activity, and indicates stability in this core funding.
findings.figures: 30.38% current collection rate vs 28.71% prior year (+1.67 percentage points)
findings.quote: The cumulative Council Tax collection rate is marginally ahead of the rate experienced for the previous year as at 30 June 2026. This is in line with the wider county and national trends.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Total usable reserves declining by £7.9m from £39.2m to £31.3m as council deploys reserves to fund capital and operational needs
findings.detail: Opening usable reserves balance is £39,185,500; projected closing balance is £31,307,400—a net drawdown of £7,878,100. Revenue reserves fall from £28.1m to £21.2m and HRA reserves fall from £2.3m to £1.5m. The council is drawing on reserves to fund its capital programme and absorb operational deficits.
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's buffer against volatility and unexpected pressures; a sustained drawdown of this scale reduces financial flexibility and raises questions about the sustainability of current spending levels.
findings.figures: £39,185,500 opening usable reserves; £31,307,400 closing; £7,878,100 total drawdown; revenue reserves £28.1m → £21.2m; HRA reserves £2.3m → £1.5m
findings.quote: The Medium Term Financial Strategy identifies the utilisation of reserves to fund the Council's priority projects.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: New Homes Bonus funding stream has ended after 15 years; council loses access to £23.2m in cumulative support received since 2011/12
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus ceased 31 March 2026. The council received NHB for 15 years (2011/12 to 2025/26), accumulating £23,232,000 in total awards. Remaining reserves of £2,387,000 are being deployed to fund capital schemes. This is a permanent loss of a recurring funding source that the council had come to rely on.
findings.matters: Loss of a recurring income stream is a structural change to council finances; £23m in cumulative support is material and its disappearance requires the council to either reduce spending or increase reliance on other income sources.
findings.figures: £23,232,000 total awarded over 15 years; £2,387,000 remaining for 2026/27
findings.quote: In total the Council has been awarded £23,232,000 up to 31 March 2026. As confirmed in the Final Local Government Finance Settlement, as expected based on the Fairer Funding Review, New Homes Bonus grants ceased 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: The Old Sidings contamination remediation costs exceeded forecast; £155,000 budget increase from Financial Resilience reserve requested
findings.detail: This town-centre site was acquired 'at risk' due to strategic value. Although contamination was anticipated, 'the extent of remediation works has increased beyond those anticipated.' Additional drainage works and specialist wildlife surveys are required; Environment Agency approval for drainage is still pending as a pre-commencement condition. The council will request a £155,000 budget increase from reserves to complete the scheme. The project underspends by £5m in 2026/27 due to programme delays.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on capital schemes indicate project management and risk estimation challenges; drawing reserves to cover unexpected costs depletes the council's financial buffer.
findings.figures: £155,000 additional budget request; £5m 2026/27 underspend
findings.quote: This site was acquired at risk due to its strategic value in the Council's plans to improve town centre facilities. Whilst contamination was anticipated and planned for in the site development, the extent of remediation works has increased beyond those anticipated. A number of factors have contributed to this including additional drainage and a specialist wildlife survey and actions to ensure the local wildlife and the river Slea are protected. A budget increase of £155,000 funded from the 'Financial Resilience' reserve will be requested to enable scheme completion.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Heart of Sleaford cinema project delayed to 2027/28 conclusion; start on site pushed to autumn 2026 for regulatory approvals
findings.detail: The major town-centre cinema scheme, originally planned to complete in 2026/27, has been rescheduled. Start on site is now autumn 2026 (later than originally planned) to allow for Environment Agency permits and enabling works to reinforce river walls. Construction will now conclude in 2027/28. The scheme underspends by £2.3m in 2026/27 as a result.
findings.matters: Delay of a flagship capital project by one year is a material strategic shift; it also signals regulatory/environmental complexity that can delay delivery and increase costs.
findings.figures: £2.3m 2026/27 underspend; schedule slipped from 2026/27 to 2027/28 completion
findings.quote: The start on site has now been scheduled for autumn 2026, later than originally planned to allow for Environment Agency permits along with enabling works to reinforce the River Slea walls around the site. The cinema construction will now conclude in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account projects operating deficit of £160,700; working balance will fall below the required minimum of £1m by £26,181
findings.detail: The HRA is in deficit on net cost of service by £160,700. This reduces contributions to the Major Repairs Reserve by £66,700 and to the Affordable Rent Reserve by £51,300. The council's policy requires an HRA working balance minimum of £1m; the opening balance was £766,500 and with only £207,200 available to add (vs the £250,000 budgeted), the closing balance will be £973,819—£26,181 below the minimum.
findings.matters: A housing revenue account in deficit is a material concern for a lender; falling below minimum reserve thresholds indicates financial stress and reduced capacity to absorb further shocks.
findings.figures: £160,700 net deficit; £1m minimum policy requirement; £766,500 opening balance; £973,819 projected closing (£26,181 shortfall); £66,700 MRR reduction; £51,300 ARR reduction
findings.quote: As at 30 June 2026, the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) showed a projected deficit on its net cost of service of £160,700 for 2026/27... As there is a projected operating deficit of £42,700 on the HRA Account, the value available to top up the working Balance is only £207,200 which would take the closing balance to £973,819 at 31 March 2027 which is marginally below it's prescribed minimum balance of £1,000,000.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Capital programme underspends by £49.1m (45% of approved budget) due to delays in major schemes; council describes this as a financial risk
findings.detail: The council approved a £109.045m capital budget in February 2026 but projects outturn of £59.903m. Major schemes experiencing delays include Heart of Sleaford cinema (now concluding 2027/28), Sleaford Moor Enterprise Park (archaeology ongoing), The Old Sidings (environmental issues), and Lafford Homes (profiling slipped). The council explicitly states: 'The delivery of a capital programme of this size represents a financial risk for the Council' and notes 'strained supply chain' conditions.
findings.matters: 45% underspend signals either over-optimistic planning or genuine delivery constraints; either way it is material to a council's ability to execute its strategic investment programme and affects the financial return on capital deployed.
findings.figures: £109.045m approved; £59.903m projected outturn; £49.141m underspend (45%); £13.105m spent/committed by 30 June
findings.quote: The delivery of a capital programme of this size represents a financial risk for the Council in order for it to see its ambitious plans being implemented to the timetables set.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: Council will borrow £38m in 2026/27, with £20m concentrated in Q4 to minimize borrowing costs; £15m replaces maturing debt
findings.detail: Of the £38m borrowing requirement, £15m replaces existing debt maturing in-year and £23m finances the capital programme. The council has already drawn £10m from the West Midlands Combined Authority and will take the remaining £28m in the second half of the year, with £20m in the final quarter. This strategy generates material borrowing cost savings; additionally, the council borrowed £4.279m less than forecast in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Substantial new borrowing is a key financial event; concentration of £20m in Q4 creates a significant liquidity event; council demonstrates active treasury management.
findings.figures: £38m total; £15m debt replacement; £23m capital financing; £10m WMCA (drawn 21 May 2026); £20m Q4 drawdown; £617,600 in-year saving; £4.279m 2025/26 underborrow
findings.quote: Our latest forecasts show that £38m of GF borrowing is required in 2026/27. Of this £38m, £15m is to replace existing borrowing which matures in year. Circa £23m is therefore for the Capital financing need for 2026/27. Apart from the £10m West Midlands Combined Authority (WMCA) borrowing already taken out on the 21 May 2026, the remaining £28m will all be taken out in the 2nd half of the financial year, with £20m being in the last quarter.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Detailed Financial Performance Report as at 30.06.26
findings.headline: General Fund projects a £533,300 surplus for 2026/27, driven primarily by Lafford Homes loan timing reducing borrowing costs
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget in February 2026 but Q1 outturn shows a £533,300 surplus, primarily because Lafford loan drawdowns are concentrated in the second half of the year rather than spread throughout. This timing defers borrowing, creating an in-year saving of £617,600 in borrowing costs. Offsetting this are a £51,400 cost-of-living pay award overspend and £22,800 in additional fleet fuel costs.
findings.matters: A surplus is better than a deficit, but a lender needs to know it is a timing benefit, not operational improvement, and whether it is repeatable.
findings.figures: £533,300 surplus; £617,600 borrowing cost saving; £51,400 pay award impact; £22,800 fuel overspend
findings.quote: The General Fund Summary is attached at Appendix 1 and, at this stage, projects a surplus of £533,300 for the financial year 2026/27.

findings.headline: Food waste collection service launched 30 March 2026 reported as successfully implemented with strong participation
findings.detail: The council's weekly food waste collection service, launched 30 March 2026 under the Environment Act 2021, has been successfully delivered with strong resident participation, positive feedback, and robust collection volumes. The report notes that operational arrangements continue to be refined and that risks and pressures continue to be monitored.
findings.matters: A new statutory service with operational and financial implications affects the council's cost base and service delivery capability; a lender needs to see that new mandated services are being delivered effectively without creating unsustainable financial stress.
findings.figures: Service launched 30 March 2026; operating through Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: The service has been successfully delivered within the statutory requirements of the Environment Act 2021 and has achieved strong levels of resident participation and satisfaction during its first quarter of operation.

findings.headline: Internal Drainage Board Levy Support grant of £314,000 not budgeted due to income uncertainty
findings.detail: An IDB Levy Support grant of £314,000 is being appropriated to the Income Volatility Reserve. This was not provided for in the original 2026/27 budget due to uncertainty around its receipt, indicating forecasting challenges with this income source.
findings.matters: Income volatility and the need for reserves to smooth uncertain grant income suggests the council faces structural income challenges that may affect its ability to fund services consistently.
findings.figures: £314,000 IDB Levy Support grant
findings.quote: That the 2026/27 Internal Drainage Board Levy Support grant allocation of £314,000 be appropriated to the Income Volatility reserve. Due to the uncertainty associated with this grant during the budget setting period, no provision for receipt of this grant was made.

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus Grant Ended, Removing 15-Year Funding Stream and Shifting Council Entirely to Local Income Sources
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus, a government grant the council received for 15 years commencing 2011/12, ceased on 31 March 2026. Total receipts over 15 years were £23.232 million. The council is now drawing these funds from reserves to support capital investment (£1.317m drawdown forecast for 2026/27 from reserves), and the NHB reserve will be depleted to £87,000 by 2028/29. This represents the loss of a material recurring revenue source, and the council now has zero government grant to support its budget.
findings.matters: This is a structural change in funding dependency. The council is now 100% reliant on council tax and business rates (which are both cyclical and exposed to local economic performance). There is no longer a central-government buffer. Coupled with the business rates collection decline already visible, this means income volatility is now entirely unhedged.

A collections shortfall directly erodes planned income.
findings.matters: With no government grant cushion, the council's income is now entirely exposed to local economic conditions. A 2.6 percentage point collection shortfall is material when it represents real income loss, and cyclical weakness in business rates signals economic stress in the local economy.
